title: Chapter 205 – The Terrace of Bells
html:
[Terrace Two – Lin Jian]

The Ferryman says nothing about the fare on the second crossing, and Jian does not ask.

He sits in the middle of the black boat with his back straight and his staff across his knees, and watches the old man's shoulders. They have changed since the first leg. They are lower now. The gray cloak hangs on them like wet canvas on a drying frame, and the long pole, when it dips, goes in a half beat late. Every stroke costs something. Jian cannot see what. He can only see the Ferryman's hands, bone-pale on the wood, and the way they tighten at the end of each thrust as though gripping a thing that might slip.

One year, he thinks. Per leg. And it comes out of the keel, or the boat, or the man.

He has done the sum a dozen times since they left Maren's kitchen. Ninety-three years and two hundred and thirteen days, less nothing, because the Ferryman has carried the fare. He cannot let it go on. At the next landing he will pay, himself, whatever is owed. That is a decision. He has made it. It sits in his chest next to the other weights, cold and plain and not especially heavy.

"You are counting," says Hua.

She sits in the bow with Mo Yan asleep against her shoulder. The lantern at the prow throws her face into planes of light and shadow, and the bandage on her hand shines like bone.

"I am always counting."

"What is it this time?"

"The cost of getting there."

"And?"

"It is going to be more than I have." He says it lightly. "But I have always been bad at arithmetic."

She does not laugh. She looks at him for a long moment with her dark, steady, unhurried eyes, and then she turns her head toward the water.

"The man with the lantern," she says. "Ye Shuhan. How long ago did he take this road?"

"Maren says nine days."

"On foot?"

"I do not think so." He frowns. "A hundred years to the Ninth Terrace, on foot. He cannot have walked it. Not unless he has stopped time. The Road of Nine is a ladder, and a ladder can be climbed quickly by a man who knows the rungs."

"Meaning he has a guide."

"Meaning he has a very good map." He turns his head. "Hua. When you opened the Roll. Did you see the Cartographer?"

"A heavy man. A stoop." She shuts her eyes. "He was in the ring. He rubbed his eyes a great deal."

"Door Nine is his."

"Yes."

"And Ye Shuhan is walking a road that a dead cartographer drew." His mouth tightens. "I would very much like to know where he got the chart."

* * *

The second landing is a bell.

It is the first thing Jian hears, long before the black water gives way to white stone. A deep round note, low as a groan, rolling out across the lake like a wave. It is followed by a second, higher, from further off, then a third, then a fourth, each slightly out of time with the last, until the whole dark vault above the boat is trembling with sound. Pebble wakes with a start in the hollow of his cloak, claws out.

What is that?

"Bells."

I can hear that. A snort. They are very bad bells.

"They are meant to be."

Why?

He does not know. But the answer comes as the boat glides in, and the bells fall silent one by one, and a white stone quay rises out of the dark.

The Second Terrace is a belfry.

That is the only word for it. A tall narrow tower of gray stone rises from the center of the landing, a hundred feet or more, and every inch of its face is hung with bells. Hundreds of them. Small ones like teacups, huge ones like cauldrons, bronze and iron and horn and glass, all swaying gently in a wind that Jian cannot feel. Each is tied to the next by a thin silver cord. The cords run up and down the tower in a network like a web. When one bell is struck, the cord pulls tight, and the next one answers.

At the foot of the tower, in a patch of trampled snow, sits an old man in a heavy gray cloak, ringing a hand bell.

"Keeper," calls the Ferryman, in his dry voice.

The old man does not look up. He is blind. That is clear at once: his eyes are two milky pools, wide open, fixed on the tower. His face is a mass of deep lines. He rings the hand bell once, twice, with a slow deliberate motion, and listens, with his whole head cocked, to the answer that comes back down the cords.

"Eleven strokes," he says. "Eleven visitors."

"Four, Orrin."

"Eleven." The old man smiles. "You are the Ferryman. I know your pole. There is a man with a staff, a woman with a mark, a child with a cat, and a thing with scales. That is four." He turns his sightless eyes toward the quay. "The other seven are above. They arrived this morning. They are being very polite."

Jian goes cold.

* * *

The seven are standing in the belfry courtyard in a neat line, and they are very polite indeed.

They wear the gray silk of the Azure Cloud Sect, brushed and pressed, with white sashes at the waist and small silver pins at the collar. They are young, between twenty and thirty, with the clean unlined faces of those who have eaten well all their lives. Each carries a sword at the hip. Each has the same watchful, bloodless composure, as though they had been cut from the same bolt of cloth. At their head stands a woman of about forty with a long jaw and cropped hair, her hand resting lightly on the hilt of her blade.

"Head Lin," she says. She bows from the waist, precisely. "I am Elder Ming Xue. Elder Ye sends his greetings."

"Elder Ye is not here."

"Elder Ye has gone ahead." She straightens. "He left us to wait for you. He said you would come."

"Did he?"

"He said that a man who could open Door Eight could not fail to follow." Her smile is thin and exact. "He admires your work."

Jian studies her. He is aware of Hua's presence at his shoulder, small and quiet and tense, and of Mo Yan's hand creeping into his sleeve. He is aware of the Ferryman standing silent on the quay behind them. He is aware of a dull, familiar tightness in his chest that says: this will go badly.

"What does Elder Ye want?" he says.

"To make friends." Ming Xue spreads her hands. "The Sect has watched this road for six centuries, Head Lin. We have kept the Hundred Stairs. We have trained our disciples to climb. We have wondered, in our hearts, what was at the top. And now it has opened, and we find that the Founders' own heirs are already here." She inclines her head. "We feel we have been rather neglected."

"You are trespassing."

"We are invited." A slight inflection. "Elder Ye holds a seal."

"A copy."

"It opens the ward."

"It opens one ward. There are nine." He keeps his voice level. "I do not think your Elder realizes what he is climbing."

"I think he realizes exactly." Ming Xue's eyes glitter. "That is why he is so very patient."

Hua steps forward. Her bandaged hand is clenched at her side, and her face is white. "Where did he get the map?"

"Map?"

"The chart of the road. A Sect that has kept a staircase for six hundred years does not know how to climb it overnight. Someone gave you a chart."

The Elder's smile does not waver. But Jian sees a muscle in her jaw tighten.

"I am afraid I do not know what you mean," she says.

"I think you do." Hua's voice is quiet. "I think someone told you that the road could be walked in nine days, if you knew the rungs. And I think that someone is dead. Or ought to be."

Ming Xue says nothing. For a long moment the courtyard is silent except for the sway of a thousand bells.

* * *

Orrin explains it later, in the belfry, with a cup of hot barley wine in his knotted hands.

They sit on the lowest landing of the tower, in a ring of wooden stools, with the Sect's seven disciples watching from the stairs. Ming Xue has withdrawn with her people to the upper gallery, courteous and unhurried, and the old man's blind face is turned toward the dark. He has the look of one listening to a conversation in the next room.

"They came yesterday," he says. "Seven of them. They said they were an advance party. They were very kind. They brought me a wineskin, and I thought: the Stair-Father's people do not bring gifts."

"What did they want?"

"To be shown the way up." He sips. "I said I could not. The bells do not guide. They warn. They tell the Keeper who is on the road, and how many, and whether they mean harm."

"And?"

"Seven came up the stair. The bells rang eleven." He is silent a moment. "Four strokes for the seven. Seven for the one who walked ahead of them. A thing I could not hear."

"Ye Shuhan."

"I do not know his name." The old man's hand tightens on the cup. "But I know a footstep. And I have never heard a man walk so softly in a place that rings."

"You think he is not alone."

"I think he is wearing something." The blind eyes turn toward the ceiling. "A thing that muffles. A thing that carries the sound away. It is as though a bell had been wrapped in cloth."

Jian sits very still. The cold in his chest has moved to his stomach.

Wrapped in cloth.

"A shroud," he says.

"I do not know the word."

"A thing used to silence a bell. In the old rites." He is thinking quickly, feeling for the shape of it, and the Interface is stirring, small and sharp, at the edge of his sight. "Orrin. If a man wanted to pass your bells unheard. If he carried the Veiled's seal and a cartographer's chart and a... muffler. What would he need to fear?"

"The great bell."

"Where is it?"

"At the top of the tower." The old man lifts a trembling finger. "It has not rung in six hundred years. The clapper was removed by the Stair-Father himself. It lies in the cellar under the stair. I am not permitted to touch it."

"Why?"

"Because it is not a bell." Orrin's face is grave. "It is a voice. It rings only once. When it does, every door on the road opens. Every door, to everyone, at once."

Hua makes a small sound. Jian does not look at her. He is looking at the old man's face, at the empty milky eyes, at the worry deep in the lines of his mouth.

"The Stair-Father built it," says Jian slowly, "so that if the Keepers ever failed, if the road were ever overrun, someone could ring it and throw the gates open. To let the people flee. To let the Bloom's pursuers in."

"Both," says Orrin. "He said it was a mercy and a curse. He said the Keeper who rang it would have to be certain."

"And Ye Shuhan knows where the clapper is."

"I do not know what he knows."

"I do." Jian rises, leaning on the staff. "Orrin. The clapper. Where, exactly, in the cellar?"

* * *

It takes the Interface eleven seconds to find it, and eleven minutes to decide what to do.

He stands in the cold stone cellar under the belfry with Mo Yan at his side and a lantern at his feet. The room is low and round and empty except for a plain iron box on a plinth. Its lid is shut. A fine film of dust lies over the top, undisturbed. A circle of pale silver is inlaid in the floor around it, hair-fine, humming.

Scan, he thinks.

```
ARK-7 // SCAN (NO COST)
OBJECT: BELL CLAPPER, THE GREAT BELL (TERRACE TWO)
MATERIAL ........ STAIR-FATHER'S SIGNATURE ALLOY
STATE ........... INTACT, SEALED (WARD, CIRCLE OF SILVER)
FUNCTION ........ MASTER KEY: OPENS ALL TERRACE WARDS
WARD STATUS ..... SOUND
TAMPER CHECK: NONE
NOTE: THE WARD HAS BEEN PROBED AND NOT BROKEN.
NOTE: THE PROBE SIGNATURE IS NOT THE SECT'S.
NOTE: THE PROBE SIGNATURE MATCHES THE SEAL.
```

He reads the last line twice. The cellar is cold.

Not the Sect's.

"Hua," he says, without turning.

She is at the foot of the stairs, a dark shape against the lamp. "Yes."

"Someone with the mark has been down here."

"Not me."

"I know. You were on a quay." He keeps his voice level. "A copy of the mark opens the outer wards. But the inner one reads the holder. It would not accept a copy. It accepted the real thing."

"I have not been here."

"No. But someone has."

The silence is long.

"There is another," says Hua at last. Her voice is thin. "There were two of us. The Warden of the Hall, and the one who took the Dock's door. I chose the eight. Ethan took the Gate. The Cartographer..." She stops. "The Cartographer carried a seal too. They all did. Nine seals, one to a Door."

"And?"

"And the Cartographer is dead. That is what I was told." She presses her fist to her mouth. "But I was told a great many things."

Jian turns. In the lantern light her face is stricken. She looks like a woman who has realized that the floor she stands on is made of something thinner than she thought.

She doesn't know, he thinks. She truly doesn't. Whoever it is has been using her mark, or a twin of it, and she has been woken in the middle.

"Ye Shuhan is not the one with the key," he says slowly. "He has the copy. He has the map. But he is not the one who opened the ward."

"Then who?"

"Someone who has been dead for six hundred years." He swallows. "And who has been waiting for the Keystone to come up the road."

* * *

They lay the trap in the dark, and it is a very small one.

Jian does not enjoy it. He has never enjoyed a trap. But he has learned, in a hundred and nineteen years and the long cold run home, that a small trap laid early is worth any number of fights, and he has the Interface, and a blind man's bells, and a mute girl who can hear what other people cannot.

The plan is simple. The Great Bell cannot be rung without the clapper. The clapper cannot be taken without breaking the ward. The ward will not break for a copy. If Ye Shuhan, or whoever walks beside him, tries to take it, the only way is to use the real mark.

So they will let him.

Hua stands in the cellar at midnight with her bandaged hand held out over the iron box, her face pale and set, and Jian watches from the shadow by the stair. Mo Yan crouches beside him, her palm flat on the stone. Orrin sits on the lowest step, one finger resting lightly on the silver cord that runs up the wall.

"He will come," says Orrin.

"How do you know?"

"He has been asking about the cellar all day." The blind man's mouth twists. "Very politely."

Jian waits. The lantern has been shuttered. The only light is the faint pale hum of the silver circle and the glow of the mark on Hua's palm, a ring of ember in the dark. He counts his breaths. At forty, he hears it.

A footstep.

It is very soft. It comes from the top of the stair, a careful, silent tread, and it descends step by step with the patience of a man who has all night. Mo Yan's hand tightens on his sleeve. Orrin's finger moves on the cord. And then, from the foot of the stair, a voice, soft and warm and unmistakably kind:

"Warden Hua. How good of you to wait."

* * *

It is not Ye Shuhan.

Jian had expected the silk gown, the polished face, the thin gray beard. He had braced for the smooth voice of a man who comforts widows. What stands at the foot of the stair is a figure in a plain gray hooded cloak, thin and stooped, with a bandaged hand held against its chest. A veil of gauze covers its face. It stops in the circle of silver light and tilts its head, and the voice that comes from beneath the gauze is not a man's, nor a woman's, but something that has been both.

"Hello, my dear," it says. "I have been waiting a long time."

Hua has gone white to the lips. "Who are you?"

"You know me."

"I do not."

"You do." The veiled figure lifts its free hand and draws back the hood. Beneath it is a face that might have been fifty or five hundred, narrow and lined and curiously blank, like a statue worn smooth by rain. The eyes are black. They are bright and tired and terribly kind. "You gave me my name, Hua. In the rain, on the day of the ring. You said I should not be named in the Roll."

"The Tenth," breathes Orrin.

"One of them." The figure smiles. "There are a great many of us, I'm afraid. The Founders were not fond of leaving things to chance."

Jian steps out of the shadow. His legs shake. He does not let it show. "You are the one who has been using the mark."

"I am the one who made the mark." The black eyes turn to him, and he sees in them a depth that makes his stomach lurch. "Hua's was the first. It was struck on the day of the ring, from a pattern I drew. But a pattern can be copied, Head Lin. And the Sect has been so very good at copying."

"You gave it to them."

"I left it where they would find it." A shrug. "It seemed kindest. They were so lonely down there."

Hua takes a step back. "You are not the Stair-Father."

"No." The voice is gentle. "I am his shadow. I am what he sent down to see who would come."

"Why?"

"Because the Stair-Father is dying, my dear. And he wishes very much to be relieved." The figure lifts its bandaged hand, and from beneath the cloth comes a pale, steady, ember glow. "I am sorry. I am afraid you have been used. All of you. But I do not think you will mind, in the end."

Jian reaches for the Interface. It has already opened.

```
ARK-7 // ALERT
UNIDENTIFIED SIGNATURE: DOOR 10 (TENTH)
PATTERN ........ INCOMPLETE (SHADOW)
HOLD ........... PRESENT, UNBOUND
WARD STATUS .... CLAPPER WARD: PROBE ACTIVE
INTENT ......... OPEN ALL DOORS
RECOMMEND: DO NOT ALLOW
```

"No," says Jian.

The shadow of the Tenth turns its head. The black eyes are wide and mild and utterly unafraid.

"No?"

"I am sorry. I have promised my sister that I will not die of something stupid." His voice shakes. "And I have promised nine children that nobody will ever be woken, or taken, or thrown open again without their consent. I am not letting you ring that bell."

"Dear boy." The voice is almost fond. "It is not for you to let."

It reaches for the box.

Mo Yan screams.

It is a thin, wordless, silver sound, the first the girl has made in her life, and it tears through the cellar like a blade. Every bell in the tower answers. The silver cords go taut. The whole belfry shrieks, a thousand voices at once, and the iron box rattles on its plinth and the circle of silver flares white and the shadow-thing in the cloak staggers back with both hands over its veiled face.

Jian does not hesitate. He has been waiting for this since the Interface first showed him the ward. He throws himself forward, staff first, and drives the head of it into the silver circle at the exact point where the probe-trace crosses the line.

The ward snaps shut.

It does not break. It closes, like a mouth. The iron box drops through the floor in a blaze of light, down and down and out of sight, and the stone knits over the hole as smoothly as water over a dropped stone. The shadow of the Tenth reels. For one second, it stands in the middle of the cellar, gray and thin and silent, with its bandaged hand extended toward a floor that is now perfectly bare.

Then it laughs.

It is a soft, tired, rueful laugh, like a man who has lost a game of chess to a child. "Well," it says. "That was clever."

"Go," says Jian. His chest is on fire. "Go back to your Stair-Father. Tell him the clapper is gone."

"And the Keystone?"

"The Keystone is not yours to command." He wipes blood from his lip. "None of us are."

The figure bows. It is a slow, courtly, curiously respectful bow, and when it rises its eyes are bright.

"I shall tell him," it says. "He will be very pleased."

And it dissolves, like a breath on a mirror, into a drift of gray motes that rises through the ceiling and is gone.

* * *

Orrin is weeping when they come back up the stair.

He sits on the bottom step with his hand bell in his lap and the tears running down his lined face, and he does not wipe them away. Above them the great tower is silent. The thousand bells hang still on their cords. A thin gray light is creeping through the high windows, the first of the dawn.

"It is gone," he says. "The great clapper."

"I'm sorry."

"No." He lifts his blind face. "I have kept that bell for fifty years. I have lain awake every night wondering whether I would be the one to ring it. Whether I would be certain." A broken laugh. "I was never going to be certain. I am a gardener's son. I am only a Keeper. And now it is gone, and I do not have to choose."

Jian sits down beside him. He has no strength left. His knees are water. His hands, in his lap, are a blur of tremor, and there is blood on his sleeve.

"It may come back," he says. "The ward is only closed. Not destroyed. The Tenth's shadow will try again."

"Then I will ring a warning."

"You will have time?"

"I have always had time." The old man smiles. "I am very good at waiting."

Hua comes down the stair with Mo Yan in her arms. The girl is asleep, or something like it, limp and pale, her fists curled. Hua lays her gently on the stone beside Jian and sits, and for a long while the three of them say nothing at all.

"She screamed," says Hua at last.

"Yes."

"She has never made a sound. Not once. Not since the day I..." Her voice cracks. "Bell says she has no voice. That the cords were damaged. In the beds."

"Perhaps they were not as damaged as Bell thought."

"Perhaps." Hua presses her palm to the girl's forehead. "Or perhaps she only needed something worth screaming for."

On the quay, the Ferryman stands waiting with his pole. The black boat rocks against the white post. Somewhere above the tower, very high up, a single bell begins to ring. It is small and clear and sweet, and it rings once, twice, three times, and Jian does not need the Interface to know what it means.

Someone is on the road.

Someone else.

He leans his head back against the cold stone. His eyes close. He thinks, with a kind of dull wonder, that for the first time since the Night of Counting, he has won something. It does not feel like winning. It feels like a very large debt, deferred, and a very small girl asleep against his arm.
